planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; the narrow columnar habit needs little corrective pruning to stay upright.

directions: Sold under the trade name Uptight, this patented boxwood selection ('Robbuxupt') grows in a tight, upright column rather than the rounded mound typical of most small-leaf boxwood. Its tiny dark green leaves hold their color through winter with little of the bronzing common in older selections. The narrow form makes it useful for vertical accents, pot specimens, and spaced hedges where a tall but slender silhouette is wanted without constant shearing. Give it well-drained soil and consistent moisture while it establishes.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; growth is slow, so expect this small mound to take many seasons to fill its space.

directions: Marketed as Baby Jade and patented under the cultivar name 'Grejade', this selection is one of the most compact forms of Japanese boxwood available, staying close to three feet tall and wide for many years. Dense, glossy, small dark-green leaves give it a fine, refined texture well suited to small gardens, edging, and tight foundation spaces where larger boxwood would quickly outgrow the spot. It prefers a bit of shade and even moisture over the hot, exposed conditions some English boxwood tolerate. Light shearing in late winter keeps the naturally dense habit even tighter.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this is a quicker-growing boxwood, so space it with its eventual height in mind.

directions: Skylight is a tall, upright hybrid from the same Better Boxwood breeding program that produced Heritage and Renaissance, bred for stronger tolerance of boxwood blight than older English or American selections. Unlike most boxwood, it grows at a noticeably faster clip while still holding dense, deep green foliage along a narrow vertical frame. Its height and columnar shape suit it to screening, backdrop plantings, or large container specimens rather than low clipped hedging. It adapts to full sun or part shade and tends to need less reshaping than comparably tall older cultivars.

common_name: Appalachian Pyramid Boxwood (Columnar Cold-Hardy English Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; site out of harsh winter wind to limit foliage bronzing.

directions: Appalachian Pyramid is a registered English boxwood selection that grows as a tight, narrow cone rather than the rounded mound of common boxwood, reaching roughly the same height and width over time. Glossy dark green leaves are paler underneath, and like most English boxwood the foliage can take on a bronze cast after exposure to full winter sun and wind. The naturally columnar shape makes it a good narrow accent or repeated vertical element along a walk without heavy shearing. It tolerates deer and rabbit browsing better than many broadleaf evergreens.
sources: American Boxwood Society — International Checklist of Cultivated Buxus

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; left unpruned it still stays a compact, dense mound.

directions: Paramus is a naturally dwarf, dense form of English boxwood that mounds to about two feet tall and wide over many years without any shearing, making it a lower-maintenance alternative to clipping standard boxwood into a similar shape. Its fine-textured, compact habit suits low edging, knot gardens, and parterres where true English boxwood 'Suffruticosa' is traditionally used but slower or less reliable. It grows in full sun to part shade and benefits from even moisture and good drainage like other English boxwood forms. Occasional light shearing keeps the mound's outline crisp.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade, spacing for its eventual width if grown as a hedge.

directions: Introduced through Girard Nurseries of Geneva, Ohio, Rochester is a broad, upright English boxwood that grows considerably taller than many of the mounding or dwarf cultivars, making it a good choice for a substantial clipped or informal hedge. Small cream-green spring flowers are inconspicuous against the dense evergreen foliage. It takes full sun to part shade and ordinary medium care, holding its shape with routine shearing once established. Deer and rabbits generally leave it alone, an advantage where other hedging shrubs get browsed.
sources: American Boxwood Society — International Registration List

common_name: Henry Shaw Boxwood (Broadly Conical English Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; allow room for its broad conical spread as it matures.

directions: Named for Henry Shaw, the nineteenth-century founder of the Missouri Botanical Garden, this English boxwood selection grows into a dense, broadly conical form rather than a flat-topped hedge shape. Over time it reaches a substantial size, so it reads better as a specimen or informal screen than as low edging. Like other English boxwood it prefers full sun to part shade with consistently moist, well-drained soil, and tolerates deer and rabbit pressure better than most broadleaf evergreens. Its inconspicuous spring flowers draw early pollinators but add little ornamental interest.
sources: The Boxwood Bulletin 25(2):43-47, American Boxwood Society

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; growth is slow, so give it time to reach its mature spread.

directions: Originating at Burncoose & South Down Nurseries in Cornwall, England, Silver Beauty is a variegated English boxwood with oblong leaves edged in an irregular creamy-silver margin, a cooler and more subtle effect than gold-edged boxwood cultivars. Growth is slow and the habit stays wider than tall, so it works well as a pale accent among darker green hedging or as a specimen near a path where its foliage pattern can be seen up close. It takes full sun to part shade and the same even moisture and good drainage other English boxwood need. Light, selective pruning preserves variegation better than hard shearing, which can expose more solid green growth.
sources: American Boxwood Society — International Registration List
